title: PowerShell (pbeesly, high integrity) opened lsass.exe with full access and read its process memory on scranton.dmevals.local
summary: On scranton.dmevals.local at 2020-05-02T03:05:16, a PowerShell.exe process (PID 2976, user DMEVALS\pbeesly, LogonId 0x372E81) opened a handle to lsass.exe (PID 736) with GrantedAccess 0x1F3FFF and 0x1FFFFF (PROCESS_ALL_ACCESS) and then performed a 0x10 'Read from process memory' access on \Device\HarddiskVolume2\Windows\System32\lsass.exe (handle 0xcb4). This is the classic LSASS memory-dump access pattern. It is part of a broader intrusion on the same host: the same PowerShell session was launched from a hidden, execution-policy-bypass PowerShell that decoded a payload from C:\Users\pbeesly\Downloads\monkey.png, and the host also ran C:\ProgramData\victim\…cod.3aka3.scr and Sysinternals sdelete64.exe to wipe artifacts. A second, similar 0x1F3FFF lsass access came from wsmprovhost.exe (PowerShell Remoting) on nashua.dmevals.local at 03:09:29 under pbeesly, indicating the same tooling was used remotely. Benign lsass accessors in the same window (svchost.exe 0x1000, WindowsAzureTelemetryService.exe/AntimalwareConfig.exe 0x1400, CollectGuestLogs.exe 0x1410) are Azure guest-agent telemetry and were excluded.

title: Credential-access tooling staged on scranton (fake .scr in C:\ProgramData\victim, sdelete64 anti-forensics) alongside the LSASS access
summary: On scranton.dmevals.local, user pbeesly executed C:\ProgramData\victim\…cod.3aka3.scr (launched by explorer.exe with /S) at 02:55:56, then enumerated the folder with 'gci C:\programdata\victim\' and deleted the file with Sysinternals sdelete64.exe at 03:02:04; further sdelete64 runs wiped Draft.Zip and SysinternalsSuite.zip. On nashua.dmevals.local the same pattern continued with C:\Windows\Temp\sdelete64.exe deleting Rar.exe and working.zip. This staging/cleanup activity brackets the LSASS memory access at 03:05:16 and shows deliberate artifact removal, consistent with a credential-theft operation. No SAM/SECURITY hive export, ntds.dit copy, or DCSync command line was observed.

title: netsh trace packet capture on scranton.dmevals.local spawned by Azure Network Watcher Agent (benign platform telemetry)
summary: The only packet-capture activity in the Windows telemetry is on scranton.dmevals.local: at 2020-05-02T03:19:17Z netsh.exe was launched with 'trace start capture=yes traceFile="C:\windows\TEMP\E7116ECA-DFE6-43C7-8FA8-8D3AC5AA8726\B91E06C5-1C7C-4830-9A76-74FA211560A7.etl"' and at 03:19:24Z with 'trace stop'. Both were created by C:\Packages\Plugins\Microsoft.Azure.NetworkWatcher.NetworkWatcherAgentWindows\1.4.1421.1\NetworkWatcherAgent\NetworkWatcherAgent.exe running as SYSTEM (creator account SCRANTON$, logon 0x3e7), i.e. the Azure Network Watcher guest agent performing a short (~7 second) diagnostic capture into the agent's own TEMP ETL file. The same agent was also seen starting as a service from services.exe and being (re)installed/started via cmd.exe ('Install /service /autoStart', 'Start /service /autoStart'), and the Azure guest agent WaAppAgent.exe was concurrently cycling its own ETW sessions with logman.exe (GAEvents, RTEvents, WindowsAzure-GuestAgent-Diagnostic). No packet-capture driver (pktmon/npcap/winpcap) was loaded (0 sysmon image-load hits), no tcpdump/windump/rawcap/dumpcap usage was found in sysmon or PowerShell script blocks, and no attacker-controlled capture tooling appears. The 7045 service installations (javamtsup.exe on scranton, PSEXESVC on nashua under user pbeesly) are not packet-capture services and are unrelated to sniffing. Zeek (2020-04-30 window, non-overlapping) shows only routine conn/ssl/dns/kerberos/smb traffic with two SSL::Invalid_Server_Cert notices and generic 'weird' events — no sniffing-related notices. Conclusion: T1040 is not evidenced as attacker activity; the capture is sanctioned Azure platform monitoring.

On scranton.dmevals.local, PowerShell.exe (PID 2976, running as SYSTEM, entity {47ab858c-e1e4-5eac-b803-000000000400}) requested lsass.exe (PID 736) with GrantedAccess 0x1F3FFF at 03:05:16.623Z and 0x1FFFFF at 03:05:16.654Z. Both call traces end in UNKNOWN(...) frames rather than a signed Windows DLL path, the classic signature of an in-memory credential-dumping routine rather than legitimate lsass access. This is the only non-system process in the dataset that requested full lsass access; all other lsass accessors were svchost.exe, wininit.exe, csrss.exe, services.exe, Defender and Azure agents. It sits inside a broader intrusion chain on scranton by user pbeesly: a hidden, encoded PowerShell launched from control.exe (02:58:44Z) that decodes a payload from C:\Users\pbeesly\Downloads\monkey.png, download of SysinternalsSuite.zip (02:59:42Z), and a later hidden encoded PowerShell spawned from a registry-stored 'Javasoft' value via hostui.exe runas (03:21:28Z).

summary: Three process-creation events for C:\Windows\System32\consent.exe were returned by both the Sysmon (event.code 1) and Security (4688) stacks, i.e. UAC elevation prompts were displayed. On scranton this fits the intrusion chain: pbeesly ran 'powershell.exe -c "Start-Process C:\Windows\System32\hostui.exe -verb runas"' from cmd.exe /c hostui.bat at 03:21:19Z, which would raise a consent prompt, and hostui.exe then spawned a hidden encoded PowerShell that read and Invoke-Expression'd a value from HKLM:\SOFTWARE\Javasoft. However, I did not retrieve the individual consent.exe events, so I cannot attribute each prompt to a specific parent process or confirm a fake/credential-harvesting prompt; consent.exe is also the legitimate Windows UAC broker. Treated as suspicious-but-unconfirmed GUI prompt activity rather than a confirmed fake credential dialog.

title: Forced-authentication artifacts (Folder\shell\open\command hijack + StartUp hostui.lnk) planted by PowerShell on scranton.dmevals.local
summary: On scranton.dmevals.local, user pbeesly ran an interactive PowerShell session (PID 3876/6868) that at 02:57:18 created HKCU\Software\Classes\Folder\shell\open\command and at 02:58:18 set its (Default) value to a hidden, execution-policy-bypassing PowerShell one-liner that decodes a payload from C:\Users\pbeesly\Downloads\monkey.png and IEXes it, plus a DelegateExecute value at 02:58:30. This is the classic T1187 'Folder' handler hijack: any user or process that opens a folder triggers the attacker command, which can be used to force authentication/credential capture. At 03:04:23 the same PowerShell wrote C:\ProgramData\Microsoft\Windows\Start Menu\Programs\StartUp\hostui.lnk (Invoke-Persistence -PersistStep 2), a shortcut in the all-users StartUp folder that executes on logon. The session also ran credential-access style functions (Get-PrivateKeys exporting certs to .pfx, Get-Clipboard, keystroke/AV checks) and anti-forensics (sdelete64). The hijack keys were removed at 02:59:15 (Remove-Item HKCU:\Software\Classes\Folder* -Recurse -Force), but the StartUp shortcut remained. Supporting context: a single NTLM network logon (4624 type 3, NtLmSsp, pbeesly, from 172.18.39.2) on scranton at 03:20:41 and LsaSrv event 6038 reporting NTLM use on the same host at 03:20:41. No WebDAV/searchConnector artifacts or attacker-controlled SMB server were observed; the forced-auth mechanism here is the local shell-handler/shortcut hijack rather than a remote UNC/WebDAV path.

title: SMB/445 and WebDAV-method traffic in the zeek window is benign infrastructure activity
summary: The zeek dataset (2020-04-30, non-overlapping with the Windows windows) shows 50 conn records to SMB ports (45 to 445, 5 to 139) and 36 HTTP records with PROPFIND/MOVE/OPTIONS methods, all between 10.0.1.4 and 192.168.0.4 observed by simplerockbuild.simplerock.lan. These are internal file-share/WebDAV-style operations between two internal hosts with no evidence of an attacker-controlled listener or credential capture, and they cannot be correlated in time with the Windows forced-authentication artifacts. Likewise, the 168 security 5156 events to 445/139 and the sysmon network connections to 445 are System-process SMB traffic to internal addresses (10.0.0.4, 10.0.1.6, link-local fe80::e40c:95b6:b0a7:6429) consistent with domain GPO/SYSVOL and ADMIN$ access, not outbound forced authentication to an external host.

On scranton.dmevals.local at 2020-05-02T02:58:44Z, control.exe ("/name Microsoft.BackupAndRestoreCenter") spawned powershell.exe PID 2976 running as DMEVALS\pbeesly at High integrity with the flags -noni -noexit -ep bypass -window hidden, decoding a payload from a bitmap (C:\Users\pbeesly\Downloads\monkey.png) and IEX-ing it. At 03:05:16Z that same PowerShell process (PID 2976, entity {47ab858c-e1e4-5eac-b803-000000000400}) opened lsass.exe (PID 736) twice with GrantedAccess 0x1F3FFF and 0x1FFFFF — full-access handles consistent with in-memory credential dumping (MiniDumpWriteDump-style read of LSASS). The CallTrace shows ntdll/KERNELBASE plus an UNKNOWN module, i.e. code not backed by a known on-disk DLL. This is the strongest T1212 signal in the dataset: an adversary-controlled PowerShell session exploiting its high-integrity token to read LSASS memory. The same session later ran Invoke-Exfil (7-Zip of Downloads to \\192.168.0.4\webdav with hardcoded creds cozy/MyCozyPassw0rd!) and Invoke-SeaDukeStage -ComputerName NASHUA, and pbeesly Kerberos TGT/TGS requests (4768/4769, RC4 0x12) were issued from 10.0.1.4 to the DC newyork.dmevals.local, consistent with use of harvested credentials.

"DownLevelDaemon") - normal indexer behaviour, not cookie access. The 162 sysmon file-creation hits matching *Cookies*/*Login Data*/*Web Data* are dominated by C:\Windows\ServiceState\EventLog\Data\lastalive0.dat / lastalive1.dat (133 events) and GroupPolicy DataStore files, i.e. substring matches on unrelated paths. No non-browser process was seen touching an Edge/Chrome/Firefox cookie or Login Data store, no 4663 object-access events on cookie paths, and no sysmon event.code 10 handle to a browser image (C139 zero hits). No MFA/2FA/authenticator content was found in any PowerShell 4104 script block, no MFA-related messages in windows.other, no 4625 failures, and no command line referencing MFA, Connect-MsolService, login.microsoftonline or any identity provider. title: No MFA request generation observed; dsregcmd hits are routine Azure AD device registration

function Invoke-BeachCleanup {
    Write-Host "[*] Cleaning up"
    Remove-Item -Path "$env:USERPROFILE\Downloads\*.pfx" -Force
    Remove-Item -Path "$env:USERPROFILE\Downloads\*.bmp" -Force
    Remove-Item -Path "$env:USERPROFILE\Downloads\*.png" -Force
    Remove-Item -Path "$env:APPDATA\OfficeSupplies.7z" -Force
}
